name of paper: LServe: Efficient Long-sequence LLM Serving with Unified Sparse Attention
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have shown remarkable potential in processing long sequences, yet efficiently serving these long-context models remains challenging due to the quadratic computational complexity of attention in the prefilling stage and the large memory footprint of the KV cache in the decoding stage. To address these issues, we introduce LServe, an efficient system that accelerates long-sequence LLM serving via hybrid sparse attention. This method unifies different hardware-friendly, structured sparsity patterns for both prefilling and decoding attention into a single framework, where computations on less important tokens are skipped block-wise. LServe demonstrates the compatibility of static and dynamic sparsity in long-context LLM attention. This design enables multiplicative speedups by combining these optimizations. Specifically, we convert half of the attention heads to nearly free streaming heads in both the prefilling and decoding stages. Additionally, we find that only a constant number of KV pages is required to preserve long-context capabilities, irrespective of context length. We then design a hierarchical KV page selection policy that dynamically prunes KV pages based on query-centric similarity. On average, LServe accelerates LLM prefilling by up to 2.9x and decoding by 1.3-2.1x over vLLM, maintaining long-context accuracy. Code is released at this https URL.

contents.AI: ### LSERVE: Streamlined Long-Sequence LLM Serving with Unified Sparse Attention**Authors**: Shang Yang1*, Junxian Guo12*, Haotian Tang1, Qinghao Hu1, Guangxuan Xiao1, Jiaming Tang1, Yujun Lin1, Zhijian Liu3, Yao Lu3, Song Han13 *[Authors marked with * contributed equally]* [Link to Project](https://hanlab.mit.edu/projects/lserve)**Abstract**: Large language models (LLMs) have made impressive strides in handling lengthy sequences, yet delivering these long-context models efficiently poses a challenge. This is largely due to the quadratic computational complexity inherent in the attention mechanism during the prefilling stage, and the extensive memory required for the key-value (KV) cache during decoding. In response, we introduce LServe, a streamlined system that enhances the efficiency of long-sequence LLM serving through hybrid sparse attention. This approach integrates hardware-friendly, structured sparsity patterns for both prefilling and decoding attention into a cohesive framework, allowing for the selective bypassing of computations on less critical tokens in a block-wise manner. LServe showcases the potential of blending static and dynamic sparsity within long-context LLM attention, yielding multiplicative speed improvements by merging these optimizations. Specifically, we adapt half of the attention heads into nearly free streaming heads for both the prefilling and decoding phases. Additionally, our findings reveal that maintaining long-context capabilities requires only a constant number of KV pages, regardless of the context length. We subsequently developed a hierarchical KV page selection strategy that dynamically trims KV pages based on their similarity to queries. On average, LServe enhances LLM prefilling speeds by up to 2.9 times and decoding by 1.3 to 2.1 times over vLLM, all while retaining long-context precision. Beyond model architectural modifications in the pre-training stage (Ainslie et al., 2023; Brandon et al., 2024), existing acceleration solutions for long-sequence LLMs primarily address efficiency from two angles. The first approach centers on KV cache quantization, where methods such as QServe (Lin et al., 2024b), KIVI (Liu et al., 2024c), and KVQuant (Hooper et al., 2024) employ low-bit quantization to reduce memory usage and I/O traffic, potentially increasing generation throughput. However, these quantization techniques do not lower the number of computations performed in the attention loop, resulting in suboptimal generation speeds as sequence lengths grow. The second approach utilizes approximate sparse attention to improve long-sequence LLM performance. For example, StreamingLLM (Xiao et al., 2023), H2O (Zhang et al., 2024c), and TOVA (Oren et al., 2024) apply static masking mechanisms to reduce attention complexity, though at the expense of accuracy in long-context tasks and irregular KV cache memory layouts. DuoAttention (Xiao et al., 2024) advances this strategy by pruning attention computations at a coarser granularity using an optimization-based approach. Other methods, such as MInference (Jiang et al., 2024b) and Quest (Tang et al., 2024), implement dynamic sparse attention to accelerate either the prefilling or decoding stage. However, these approaches do not reduce KV cache memory consumption and lack a unified framework to address efficiency challenges in both stages simultaneously. To this end, we introduce LServe, an efficient system for serving long-sequence LLMs that leverages hybrid sparse attention. Recognizing that not all tokens hold equal importance, LServe integrates multiple hardware-friendly, structured sparsity patterns into a unified block sparse attention framework (see Figure 4). Block-level sparsity accelerates attention computation by processing the KV history in discrete blocks. By skipping blocks, we directly reduce the number of sequential iterations, resulting in measured speedups during both the prefilling and decoding stages. Building on the unified block sparse attention framework, LServe further illustrates acceleration opportunities from static and dynamic sparsity. For static sparsity, inspired by DuoAttention (Xiao et al., 2024), we modify the attention masks in the original model by converting half of the attention heads into Λ-shaped masks, transforming these attention heads into streaming heads. Additionally, we fuse the computation of streaming and standard attention heads into unified GPU kernels for both the prefilling and decoding stages, translating theoretical computation and memory savings that translate to up to 1.7× measured speedup. For dynamic sparsity, we observe that query-centric sparsity (Tang et al., 2024) allows for nearly lossless KV compression: the required number of KV tokens to maintain long-context capabilities remains constant (e.g., 4096), regardless of context length. To optimize efficiency, we design a hierarchical page selector to identify important KV pages for each query token, reusing the selection results across tokens to reduce page selection overhead by 4×. Our key observation is that static and dynamic sparsity patterns are orthogonal in long-sequence LLMs. By unifying static and dynamic sparsity with KV cache quantization into a single GPU kernel, LServe achieves compounded efficiency benefits from each individual optimization for decoding stage attention. We benchmark LServe across three long-sequence LLMs-Llama-3-8B, Minitron-4B, and Llama-2-7B-at context lengths up to 512k tokens. Compared to stateof-the-art frameworks like vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023b), QServe (Lin et al., 2024b), MInference (Jiang et al., 2024b), and DuoAttention (Xiao et al., 2024), LServe accelerates prefilling stage by up to 2.9× and achieves an average of 1.3×-2.1× speedup in the decoding stage. Furthermore, LServe accomplishes these speedups while retaining the long-context capabilities of the original dense, floating-point models, demonstrating that hybrid attention sparsity is a free lunch for long-sequence LLM serving. 2 BACKGROUND AND MOTIVATION 2.1 Background LLM Inference. LLMs are transformer-based architectures with stacked identical layers, each containing attention blocks, feed-forward networks (FFN), and normalization components. LLM inference involves two stages: an initial prefilling stage that handles multiple tokens concurrently, followed by auto-regressive decoding stage where only one token will be processed for each request in a decoding step.

contents.human: In LLM serving, the generation length of each sequence is highly variable and unpredictable. Padding all sequences to the maximum length results in considerable memory waste and fragmentation. To address this, vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023b) introduces PagedAttention, a KV cache management algorithm inspired by operating systems’ virtual memory. Instead of allocating a continuous memory buffer for each sequence’s KV cache, PagedAttention partitions the cache into fixed-size blocks (or pages), each holding KV data for a set number of consecutive tokens (typically 16 to 64). A page block table records the physical address of each page, allowing the PagedAttention kernel to use indirect addressing to retrieve KV features. TensorRT-LLM (NVIDIA, 2023) and QServe (Lin et al., 2024b) implement quantized page attention to reduce memory bandwidth usage during the decoding stage, resulting in further generation speedups. 2.2 Motivation Serving long-sequence LLMs is challenging due to the high cost of attention. According to QServe (Lin et al., 2024b), the ratio of attention kernels in end-to-end runtime will increase as the batch size scale up. Therefore, in real-world serving scenarios, optimizing the attention becomes increasingly critical. This approach leads to our unified block sparse attention formulation, where attention computation is skipped in a blockwise manner. LServe also supports weight, activation and KV quantization, which significantly improves generation throughput at shorter context lengths. 3.1 Unified Block Sparse Attention As shown in Figure 3, skipping computations in the attention kernel by blockwise processing accelerates execution by shortening the sequential loop. Building on this, we introduce a unified block sparse attention pattern for both the prefilling and decoding stages: each thread block computes a TQ × TK tile (and TK × TV ) in parallel. Here, TQ > 1 in the prefilling stage and TQ = 1 in the decoding stage, with TK (or TV ) corresponding to the page size in PagedAttention (Kwon et al., 2023a). We define block sparsity in LServe as follows: for each TQ × TK tile in the attention calculation, it is either fully skipped (Figure 4(b), light gray blocks) or retained as in standard causal attention (Figure 4(b), blue blocks). Given that each GPU streaming multiprocessor can execute only a limited number of thread blocks simultaneously, the attention kernel execution time can be approximated by the total count of TQ × TK (and TK × TV ) blocks. With a block sparsity of r, where rN of the N total blocks are empty, the theoretical speedup from block sparse attention is 1/(1 -r). For example in Figure 4(b), 10 out of N=21 blocks are non-empty. Thus, the theoretical speedup ratio is 2.1×. Figure 4(c)(d) shows two sparsity patterns used in LServe. The first is streaming attention (Figure 4(c)), a specialized form of block-sparse attention where each token only attends to its immediate neighbors and initial tokens, known as attention sinks (Xiao et al., 2023). Unlike dense attention, where computation for each row scales with the token index, streaming attention keeps the computation for each token constant-in this case, only two local blocks and one sink block, as shown in Figure 4(c). This pattern is nearly costfree in applications with extremely long contexts. Because streaming attention follows a fixed pattern, we designate which heads use it in offline, and make it static for different input sequences in both prefilling and decoding. The second type of sparsity, illustrated in Figure 4(d), is page sparsity, which is specifically designed for the decoding stage where TQ = 1 applies to both skipped and selected pages. Unlike streaming attention, page sparsity in LServe is dynamic, allowing different query tokens to attend to different KV pages. As noted in Deja Vu (Liu et al., 2023), dynamic sparsity results in higher compression ratios than static sparsity. Our observations indicate that static sparsity offers up to a 2× efficiency gain, whereas dynamic sparsity bounds the decoding complexity to a constant, with each query attending only to a fixed number of KV tokens. 3.2 LServe System Overview We present an overview of LServe in Figure 5. Built on QServe, which natively supports quantized LLMs, LServe enhances the baseline system by introducing sparsity into both prefilling and decoding dataflows. The two-way paged KV cache serves as the bridge between these two stages. As discussed in Section 3.1, we statically partition the attention heads of a pretrained LLM into two groups: dense heads and streaming heads. Unlike conventional LLM serving systems, which maintain a single KV cache, we utilize separate KV caches for the dense and streaming heads. The KV cache for the streaming heads is organized similarly to the pages in QServe, with scaling factors and zero points stored immediately after the token features. Additionally, the KV cache for the dense heads includes key statistics that facilitate critical page selection during the decoding stage. In the prefilling stage, the key differences between LServe and conventional dense-attention LLM serving systems are twofold: (1) we replace the dense attention kernel with our unified block sparse attention kernel, and (2) we write back quantized KV features using two distinct kernels. In the decoding stage, our system incorporates dynamic attention sparsity. Rather than developing an entirely new dynamic sparse attention kernel, we decompose the problem into two components: (1) dynamic page selection and (2) a dense attention kernel with shorter page tables, where the shorter page tables are provided by the page selector. Notably, our page selector employs hierarchical paging and reusable page selection, enhancing both long-context accuracy and page selection efficiency. contents.AI: In LLM deployment, one of the major challenges is the unpredictable variation in the length of each sequence generated. If we pad every sequence to its maximum possible length, it results in significant memory wastage and fragmentation. To tackle this issue, vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023b) introduced PagedAttention, an innovative KV cache management algorithm inspired by the concept of virtual memory in operating systems. Rather than allocating a continuous block of memory for the KV cache of each sequence, PagedAttention breaks the cache into fixed-size blocks or pages. Each of these pages contains KV data for a specific number of consecutive tokens, generally ranging from 16 to 64. A page block table keeps track of each page’s physical address, allowing the PagedAttention kernel to employ indirect addressing for retrieving KV features. To further enhance efficiency, TensorRT-LLM (NVIDIA, 2023) and QServe (Lin et al., 2024b) utilize quantized page attention during the decoding phase, which minimizes memory bandwidth usage and speeds up the generation process.When serving long-sequence LLMs, the high computational cost of attention poses significant challenges. Figure 2 illustrates how the latency breaks down for Llama-3-8B at a batch size of 1, across different sequence lengths, on an A100 GPU. As sequences exceed 64k in length, attention kernels consume at least 50% of runtime, climbing to 75% at 128k. According to QServe (Lin et al., 2024b), the proportion of attention kernels in the overall runtime will increase with larger batch sizes. Thus, optimizing attention is critical in real-world serving scenarios. Accelerating attention for long-sequence LLMs necessitates a comprehensive understanding of GPU attention kernel implementations, as depicted in Figure 3.In the prefilling phase, query tokens iterate over all key and value tokens in a block-by-block manner. Reducing KV block iterations accelerates attention directly. The attention kernel is parallelized across batch sizes, attention heads, and query tokens, with a single query token in the decoding stage. Although calculations within a block can be skipped, speed gains are minimal due to the lockstep execution of threads in a GPU warp, which causes faster threads to wait for slower ones. Therefore, a more effective strategy to accelerate attention is to reduce sequential iterations along the KV token dimension, leading to our unified block sparse attention formulation. In this setup, computation is either fully executed or skipped during the prefilling stage, except for the most recent KV block. During decoding, each sequence has only one query token, narrowing each orange-contoured grid to a 1×P dimension, where P denotes the number of KV tokens per page. We will elaborate on LServe’s sparsity pattern selection in Section 3. Additionally, because the decoding phase is memory-bound, KV cache quantization also enhances speed. While quantization reduces iteration runtime, sparsity minimizes iteration count.Introducing LServe, a robust long-sequence LLM serving system featuring unified sparse attention. LServe effectively incorporates different sparse attention patterns into a single block-sparse framework, as depicted in Figure 4, using fused CUDA kernels. Furthermore, it supports weight, activation, and KV quantization, which markedly boost generation throughput at shorter context lengths.Unified Block Sparse Attention builds on the concept of skipping attention kernel computations via blockwise processing to accelerate execution by reducing the sequential loop. This involves computing a TQ × TK tile (and TK × TV) in parallel, where TQ is greater than 1 in the prefilling stage and equals 1 in the decoding stage, with TK or TV corresponding to PagedAttention’s page size (Kwon et al., 2023a). In LServe, block sparsity is defined such that each TQ × TK tile is either fully skipped (light gray blocks in Figure 4(b)) or retained as in standard causal attention (blue blocks in Figure 4(b)). Each GPU streaming multiprocessor can only run a limited number of thread blocks at once, so attention kernel execution time is roughly proportional to the total number of TQ × TK (and TK × TV) blocks. With a block sparsity rate of r, where rN of the N total blocks are empty, the theoretical speedup from block sparse attention is 1/(1 - r). For instance, in Figure 4(b), 10 out of N=21 blocks are filled, yielding a theoretical speedup ratio of 2.1×.Figure 4(c)(d) highlights two sparsity patterns used in LServe. The first, streaming attention (Figure 4(c)), is a form of block-sparse attention where each token interacts only with its immediate neighbors and initial tokens, known as attention sinks (Xiao et al., 2023). In contrast to dense attention, which scales with token index, streaming attention maintains constant computation per token-only two local blocks and one sink block, as shown in Figure 4(c). This pattern is virtually cost-free for applications with very long contexts. Since streaming attention follows a fixed pattern, the heads using it are determined offline and remain static for various input sequences in both the prefilling and decoding stages. The second sparsity type, depicted in Figure 4(d), is page sparsity, tailored for the decoding stage where TQ = 1 applies to both skipped and selected pages. Unlike streaming attention, page sparsity in LServe is dynamic, permitting different query tokens to attend to distinct KV pages. Dynamic sparsity, as noted in Deja Vu (Liu et al., 2023), achieves higher compression ratios than static sparsity. Our findings reveal that static sparsity can double efficiency, while dynamic sparsity limits decoding complexity to a constant, with each query attending to a fixed number of KV tokens.LServe System Overview, shown in Figure 5, outlines LServe, which builds upon QServe’s support for quantized LLMs by incorporating sparsity into both prefilling and decoding dataflows. A two-way paged KV cache bridges these stages. As described in Section 3.1, we divide the attention heads of a pretrained LLM into two groups: dense and streaming heads. Unlike traditional LLM systems with a single KV cache, we maintain separate KV caches for dense and streaming heads. The streaming heads’ KV cache mirrors the pages in QServe, with scaling factors and zero points stored immediately after token features. Additionally, the dense heads’ KV cache includes key statistics for selecting critical pages during decoding.In the prefilling stage, LServe deviates from conventional dense-attention systems in two primary ways: (1) replacing the dense attention kernel with our unified block sparse attention kernel, and (2) writing back quantized KV features using two distinct kernels. In the decoding stage, our system integrates dynamic attention sparsity. Instead of creating a new dynamic sparse attention kernel, we break down the problem into dynamic page selection and a dense attention kernel with shorter page tables provided by the page selector. Our page selector employs hierarchical paging and reusable page selection, enhancing long-context accuracy and page selection efficiency.

contents.human: Sparse Attention. BigBird (Zaheer et al., 2020) reduces attention complexity by blending local, global, and random attention masks. Subsequent methods like StreamingLLM (Xiao et al., 2023), H2O (Zhang et al., 2024c), and TOVA (Oren et al., 2024) simplify attention patterns by discarding KV caches mid-way through the context. However, these approaches struggle to retain the original models’ long-context capabilities due to limited global context modeling. Recent works like DuoAttention (Xiao et al., 2024), RetrievalAttention (Liu et al., 2024a), and SeerAttention (Gao et al., 2024) address this issue by introducing retrieval heads (Wu et al., 2024) or combining full attention with local attention heads. Quest (Tang et al., 2024) introduces dynamic, query-aware sparsity for accelerated decoding, while MInference (Jiang et al., 2024b) extends similar ideas to the prefilling stage. FastGen (Ge et al., 2023) optimizes decoding by profiling attention heads to discard tokens. PQCache (Zhang et al., 2024a) and ShadowKV (Sun et al., 2024) further advance the selective attention methods with product quantization and low-rank decomposition. Additionally, LongLoRA (Chen et al., 2023) finetunes shortcontext LLMs to long-context ones after converting global attention to shifted sparse attention. 7 CONCLUSION We introduce LServe, an efficient serving system for longsequence LLMs that leverages hybrid sparse attention. By incorporating unified block sparse attention, we achieve significant acceleration of the attention mechanism for both LServe: Efficient Long-sequence LLM Serving with Unified Sparse Attention 12 prefilling and decoding stages in long-sequence models. We further show that head-level static sparsity and query-aware dynamic sparsity are orthogonal and can be effectively combined with minimal impact on accuracy. LServe surpasses state-of-the-art systems, delivering an average of 1.3×-2.1× speedup in the decoding stage and up to 2.9× speedup in the prefilling stage, preserving the models’ long-context capabilities. contents.AI: Sparse Attention is an area that has seen innovative developments over the years. One noteworthy advancement is BigBird (Zaheer et al., 2020), which decreases the complexity of attention by integrating local, global, and random attention masks. More recent methodologies, such as StreamingLLM (Xiao et al., 2023), H2O (Zhang et al., 2024c), and TOVA (Oren et al., 2024), aim to streamline attention patterns by removing key-value caches partway through the context. Despite their innovations, these techniques often fall short in maintaining the long-context capabilities of the original models due to their limited ability to model global context effectively. To tackle this challenge, recent studies like DuoAttention (Xiao et al., 2024), RetrievalAttention (Liu et al., 2024a), and SeerAttention (Gao et al., 2024) have introduced retrieval heads (Wu et al., 2024) or a combination of full attention with local attention heads. Another approach, Quest (Tang et al., 2024), employs dynamic, query-aware sparsity to speed up the decoding process, while MInference (Jiang et al., 2024b) applies similar concepts during the prefilling phase. FastGen (Ge et al., 2023) further optimizes decoding by analyzing attention heads to eliminate unnecessary tokens. Selective attention methods have also been advanced by PQCache (Zhang et al., 2024a) and ShadowKV (Sun et al., 2024) through the use of product quantization and low-rank decomposition techniques. Meanwhile, LongLoRA (Chen et al., 2023) adapts short-context large language models (LLMs) for long-context applications by converting global attention into shifted sparse attention.In our conclusion, we present LServe, an efficient system designed for serving long-sequence LLMs that utilizes hybrid sparse attention. By incorporating unified block sparse attention, LServe significantly accelerates the attention mechanism for both the prefilling and decoding stages of long-sequence models. We demonstrate that static sparsity at the head level and dynamic sparsity that is query-aware are complementary and can be combined effectively without a substantial loss in accuracy. LServe outperforms existing state-of-the-art systems, offering a 1.3× to 2.1× speedup in the decoding stage and up to a 2.9× speedup in the prefilling stage, all while maintaining the models’ ability to handle long contexts.ACKNOWLEDGEMENTSOur gratitude goes to the MIT-IBM Watson AI Lab, the MIT AI Hardware Program, the MIT Amazon Science Hub, the National Science Foundation, and Hyundai for their support of this research. name of paper: Does Ideological Polarization Lead to Policy Polarization?
summary: I analyze an election involving two parties who are both officeand policy-motivated and who are ideologically polarized. One party may possess a valence advantage. The parties compete by proposing policies on a second policy issue. The analysis reveals a subtle relationship between ideological polarization and policy polarization. If ideologies are highly dispersed, there is a U-shaped relationship between ideological polarization and platform polarization. In contrast, if ideological dispersion is limited, increasing ideological polarization generally results in policy moderation. In both cases, valence plays no role in policy polarization. Finally, as in Buisseret and van Weelden (2022), adding ideological polarization adds nuance on the effects of increasing valence: both highand low-valence candidates may adopt more extreme positions, depending on the electorate’s degree of ideological polarization.

contents.AI: Political parties often find themselves vying for support by presenting proposals on multiple policy fronts. A close examination uncovers a nuanced interaction between ideological and policy polarization. When ideological views are widely spread, a U-shaped correlation emerges between ideological polarization and platform polarization. Conversely, in scenarios where ideological variation is minimal, an increase in ideological polarization tends to lead to more moderate policy positions. Notably, in both situations, valence does not influence policy polarization. Building on the work of Buisseret and Van Weelden (2022), the introduction of ideological polarization provides additional insight into how heightened valence affects candidates: depending on the electorate’s level of ideological polarization, candidates with either high or low valence might gravitate towards more extreme positions. For instance, Abramowitz and Saunders (2008) highlight the significant rise in ideological polarization among both the general public and political elites in the United States. Similarly, Boxell, Gentzkow, and Shapiro (2024) have documented a growing polarization trend since the 1980s in countries such as the US, Canada, Switzerland, France, and New Zealand. Carothers and O’Donohue (2019) note a similar trend in places like Kenya, Indonesia, Turkey, and Poland. While it is widely believed that this growing polarization can be detrimental to the effectiveness of democratic decision-making-by making it harder for parties to compromise or learn from one another-the impact of polarization among social groups on policy development remains ambiguous. Should we anticipate that increased polarization leads to more polarized policies, or is another outcome more likely? Empirical data on this topic is unclear. Figure 1 displays both affective polarization (left panel) and policy polarization (right panel) in the US from 1998 onwards. It shows that while affective polarization has steadily increased, policy polarization initially declined before beginning to rise around 2008. This paper employs game theory to analyze how affective polarization affects policy polarization. Political parties, motivated by both their desire for office and policy outcomes, navigate an ideological spectrum to decide which policies to present to voters in their quest for election. Affective polarization was measured by the difference in average DW nominate scores between Republicans and Democrats in the House and Senate, whereas policy polarization was derived from the disparity in the rile variable for Republicans and Democrats in the Manifesto Project Database (Lehmann, Franzmann, Al-Gaddooa, Burst, Ivanusch, Regel, Riethmüller, Volkens, Weßels, and Zehnter, 2024).

contents.human: I show that increasing ideological polarization always decreases platform polarization if ideological polarization is low. When ideological polarization is large, then the effect of increasing it depends on how dispersed ideologies are: if ideological dispersion is low, then further increasing ideological polarization at some point will lead to perfect convergence in policies at the center of the policy space. However, in a society with highly dispersed ideologies, increasing polarization further leads to increasing policy polarization as well. Hence, the relationship between affective polarization and policy polarization is U-shaped as in Figure 1. The paper also shows that changing valence levels has no effect on policy polarization in any interior equilibrium. However, valence levels, together with affective polarization, determine which party adopts a more extreme and which a more centrist position. Therefore, just as in Buisseret and Van Weelden (2022), adding polarization as a determinant of policy choices adds significant nuance to the model’s predictions, and valence and policy congruence could be both positively and negatively correlated. Literature: The paper contributes to a wide array of literature in political economy. First and foremost, it contributes to the literature studying the determinants of polarization of policies. Alesina and Rosenthal (2000) show that if policies are determined by a executivelegislative compromise, voter behavior tends to moderate policies, which in turn creates incentives to choose more radical policy platforms. Polborn and Snyder (2017) show that polarization may increase in legislative competition if elections outcomes become more uncertain. Prummer (2020) shows that a more fragmented media landscape leads to an increase in polarization when parties can micro-target voters during a campaign. Similarly, Balart, Casas, and Troumpounis (2022) study how modern information technology, that allows for more precise targeting of voters during an electoral campaign, may induce policy polarization. Yuksel (2022) shows that in fractionalized societies polarization of policies tends to be greater when voters need to spend time to learn about policy parties’ multi-dimensional platforms. Matakos, Troumpounis, and Xefteris (2015, 2016) study how different degrees of rule-disproportionality of electoral systems affect policies. Levy and Razin (2015) show that greater polarization of opinions caused by correlation neglect may lead to less polarization of policies. Denter (2021) shows that greater valence leads to policy moderation if there are complementarities between policy and valence. In contrast to all of these paper, the focus in the current paper is how ideological polarization impacts policies. The paper also contributes to the literature studying the implications of differences in valence, pioneered by Stokes (1963). Ansolabehere and Snyder (2000), Groseclose (2001), 3 and Aragones and Palfrey (2002) study models of electoral competition and policy motivated candidates and show that candidates with a valence advantage tend to choose more moderate positions that their disadvantages counterparts. A very closely related paper is Buisseret and Van Weelden (2022). They enrich the model of electoral competition between office motivated candidates by introducing fixed candidate ideology as a third characteristic. Their analysis reveals that if the weight of ideology in voters utility function is high enough, i.e., if societies are polarized, then the standard result in the literature that the candidate with the valence advantage takes the more moderate position may change. That is similar to the analysis in Xefteris (2014), who extends the classical model to three candidates and shows that when there is significant uncertainty about voters’ preferences, then the candidate with the greatest valence may choose the most extreme policy position. Aragones and Xefteris (2017), consider a model in which voters may be heterogeneous in how they evaluate candidates’ non-policy characteristics. They demonstrate that policy polarization follows a U-shaped pattern concerning the proportion of voters supporting the more popular candidate. The current paper is closely related to Buisseret and Van Weelden (2022), but allows for policy motivation on the candidates’ side and uncertainty about the election outcome draws not from uncertainty about voters bliss points but from aggregate shows to the share of voters supporting a given candidate. The analysis reveals that valence has no impact whatsoever on policy polarization, but it determines which candidates locates closer to the political center. If societies are sufficiently polarized, then the candidate or party with the valence advantage may take a less extreme position. Finally, the paper contributes to the literature studying electoral competition when positions on a subset of policy issues are fixed. The pioneering article in this field is due to Krasa and Polborn (2010), in which they study a model of electoral competition with office-motivated candidates. There are multiple binary policy issues, and candidates are exogenously committed to fixed positions on some issues while choosing positions on the remaining ones. Buisseret and Van Weelden (2020) consider a variant of their model with two issues and two incumbent politicians, who hold fixed and opposing positions on one of these dimensions and can freely choose policies in the other. The novelty in their model is that they allow for an outsider candidate to challenge the incumbents. They show that the incumbents are particularly vulnerable to the entry of the outsider when ideological polarization is high. Hughes (2024) also considers a variant of Krasa and Polborn (2010) to study strategic voting in legislative elections. He shows that in legislative elections equilibrium policies are both more predictable and more representative of voter preferences than in sin4 gle district elections. The current paper differs in that, while parties occupy fixed ideological positions, they are free to choose policy in a second, continuous policy dimension. The focus is thereby to highlight how ideological polarization impacts the polarization of policies.
contents.AI: I demonstrate that when ideological polarization is initially low, increasing it always leads to a decrease in platform polarization. However, once ideological polarization reaches a high level, the effect of further increasing it depends on the spread of ideological beliefs. In scenarios where ideological dispersion is minimal, boosting ideological polarization even more eventually causes policies to converge perfectly at the center of the policy spectrum. On the other hand, in societies with a wide range of ideologies, further polarization leads to an increase in policy polarization. Consequently, the relationship between affective polarization and policy polarization forms a U-shape, as depicted in Figure 1. Additionally, the study finds that altering valence levels has no impact on policy polarization in any stable equilibrium. Nonetheless, valence levels, combined with affective polarization, influence whether a party chooses a more extreme or a more centrist stance. Thus, similar to Buisseret and Van Weelden (2022), incorporating polarization as a factor in policy decisions introduces considerable complexity to the model’s forecasts, suggesting that valence and policy alignment can be either positively or negatively related.The paper makes significant contributions to a broad spectrum of political economy literature. Primarily, it adds to the body of work examining the factors that drive policy polarization. Alesina and Rosenthal (2000) found that when policies result from an executive-legislative compromise, voter behavior tends to moderate these policies, which paradoxically encourages more radical policy platforms. Polborn and Snyder (2017) argued that legislative competition might heighten polarization if election outcomes become unpredictable. Prummer (2020) noted that a fragmented media landscape can amplify polarization when parties are able to micro-target voters during campaigns. Similarly, Balart, Casas, and Troumpounis (2022) analyzed how advancements in information technology that enable precise voter targeting during elections may cause policy polarization. Yuksel (2022) highlighted that in divided societies, policy polarization often intensifies as voters take time to understand parties’ complex platforms. Matakos, Troumpounis, and Xefteris (2015, 2016) explored how varying degrees of rule disproportionality in electoral systems influence policies. Levy and Razin (2015) indicated that increased opinion polarization from correlation neglect could result in less policy polarization. Denter (2021) suggested that greater valence might lead to more moderate policies when policy and valence are complementary. Unlike these studies, my paper zeroes in on the influence of ideological polarization on policy outcomes. Moreover, this paper contributes to the literature on valence differences, a field pioneered by Stokes (1963). Ansolabehere and Snyder (2000), Groseclose (2001), and Aragones and Palfrey (2002) examined electoral competition models and showed that candidates with a valence advantage often choose more moderate positions compared to their disadvantaged counterparts. A closely related work is by Buisseret and Van Weelden (2022), who expanded the model of electoral competition by incorporating fixed candidate ideology. Their findings reveal that if ideology holds significant weight in voters’ utility functions, particularly in polarized societies, the conventional result that candidates with a valence edge adopt more moderate positions may not hold true. This echoes Xefteris (2014), who extended the classical model to three candidates, showing that substantial uncertainty about voter preferences can lead the candidate with the highest valence to choose the most extreme policy stance. Aragones and Xefteris (2017) considered a model where voters vary in their evaluation of candidates’ non-policy traits, demonstrating that policy polarization follows a U-shape relative to the proportion of voters backing the leading candidate.This paper, akin to Buisseret and Van Weelden (2022), examines policy motivation in candidates alongside electoral uncertainty, which arises not from uncertainties about voters’ ideal points but from the aggregate share of voter support. The study reveals that valence itself does not affect policy polarization, but it does influence which candidate gravitates closer to the political center. In deeply polarized societies, the candidate or party with a valence advantage may take a less extreme position. Lastly, the paper advances the literature on electoral competition when positions on certain policy issues are fixed. Krasa and Polborn (2010) pioneered this field, studying models with office-driven candidates committed to fixed positions on some issues while being free to choose others. Buisseret and Van Weelden (2020) expanded on this by including an outsider candidate challenging incumbents with fixed positions, finding that incumbents are particularly susceptible to such challenges in highly polarized environments. Hughes (2024) adapted Krasa and Polborn’s model to examine strategic voting in legislative elections, demonstrating that policies are more predictable and representative of voter preferences in these elections compared to single-district ones. My paper diverges by allowing parties to maintain fixed ideological positions while freely selecting policies in a second, continuous policy dimension, focusing on how ideological polarization affects policy polarization.

We first consider the case when no candidate has an advantage because of either voter preferences or valence, v = 0 and μ1 = μ2 = 1 2. In this case, a symmetric equilibrium exists in which parties choose platforms symmetrically around the preferred point of the median in dimension 2, i.e., pL 2 = 1 -pR 2 , and both parties win with an equal probability of 50 percent. To get a better intuition for how ideological polarization influences policy platforms, assume first that the first dimension is irrelevant, w = 0. Then we have a classical one-dimensional electoral competition model without ideological polarization. Parties intent to appeal to the median in the second issue dimension, without deviating to far from their own preferred policies. Assumption 1 guarantees that this equilibrium is interior, pL 2 ∈(0, 1 2). Now assume w increases by a bit, and therefore society becomes a little more polarized. Should we expect parties to move closer to their own preferred policies or to become more moderate? To answer this, we need to shed more light on the different channels through which such a change affects parties’ strategies. On the one hand, choosing policies closer to the own ideal will be punished somewhat less by the electorate, because when w > 0, parties are not judged solely based on their policies in dimension 2. On the other hand, when w increases, then, for any (pL 2 , pR 2 ), parties become more office motivated, because they dislike losing more for ideological reasons. Because deviations from the symmetric equilibrium lead to only second-order changes of winning probabilities, but to first-order changes in incentives through greater polarization, parties become more moderate when w is small and increases. But what happens when society is ideologically extremely polarized, i.e., if w is large? In this case, we may hypothesize, that small differences in policies in dimension 2 have little effect on winning probabilities. But does this imply that parties move all the way to their own preferred policies, hence taking extreme policy platforms, and policy polarization increases? If ideologies are not only important but also highly dispersed, then most voters have extreme ideologies and thus have a clear party preference based on ideology alone. Then the marginal effect of moving closer to the center of dimension 2 on the winning probability vanishes, and 7 accordingly parties indeed choose extreme policy platforms in dimension 2. However, if ideologies are important, but voters are relatively homogeneous in their ideologies, then most voters have no strong preference based on parties’ ideologies. The marginal change in the winning probability from changing the dimension 2 policy is identical for both. In other words, both the stronger and the weaker party may choose a more centrist stance. This is in contrast to a large body of literature, that predicts that the advantaged party locates closer to the expected median than the contender, at least if the advantage is not too large. This is what Groseclose (2001) coined the moderating frontrunner effect. Buisseret and Van Weelden (2022) show that this effect may not be present anymore when there is ideological polarization. When one party has more core supporters than the other based on the ideological dimension 1, then this party may be the stronger party despite a valence disadvantage. Hence, if the weight on ideology is low, the difference in valence determines which party is stronger and hence also which party locates closer to the political center of dimension 2. However, if ideology becomes very important, at one point this changes and a party might locate closer to the political center despite having a (small) valence disadvantage. Parties that are both office and policy motivated and that are polarized along an ideological dimension choose which policies to offer to voters in an effort to get elected. I show that increasing ideological polarization always decreases platform polarization if ideological polarization is low. When ideological polarization is large, then the effect of increasing it depends on how dispersed ideologies are: in a society with highly dispersed ideologies, increasing polarization further leads to increasing policy polarization as well. However, if ideological dispersion is low, then further increasing ideological polarization at some point will lead to perfect convergence in policies at the center of the policy space. The paper also shows that changing valence levels has no effect of policy polarization in any interior equilibrium. However, valence levels, together with ideological polarization, determine which party adopts a more extreme and which a more centrist position. Just as in Buisseret and Van Weelden (2022), adding ideological polarization to the model adds significant nuance to its predictions, and valence and policy congruence could be both positively and negatively correlated. In the concluding section of this paper, I explore how differences in ideological polarization and valence affect policy polarization within a game theoretic framework.
